lines: A compliance team wants years of history kept around, fully readable.
Priced on the broker's own disk, that bill is simply absurd.
Move the old, closed part of the log somewhere cheaper, and the same years of history stay readable for a fraction of the cost.
Picture the same strip this chapter keeps coming back to, with one new boundary drawn across it.
Past that boundary, the older material now lives in object storage instead.
Before it, the newest material still sits exactly where it always has, on the broker's own disk.
Worth reasoning through before the reveal settles it.
A segment has just finished closing.
Does moving it to cheaper storage wait until local space is actually running short, or does that move start right away?
answer: It starts right away, the instant the segment closes.
Nothing about local disk running short needs to happen first.
A dedicated piece of the broker watches for exactly this moment and begins the copy immediately.

lines: So there are really two separate clocks here, not one.
The copy begins the moment a segment closes.
Deleting that segment's local copy only happens afterward, once a separate local-retention window has run out on top of that.
Worth reasoning through before the next reveal settles it.
A consumer asks for an old offset using the exact same call it always uses.
From that call alone, can it tell whether the answer is about to come from local disk, or from somewhere much farther away?
answer: No, it genuinely can't tell from the call itself.
The request looks identical either way.
Only how long the answer takes to arrive gives away which one actually served it.

lines: Here's that exact gap, measured rather than assumed.
A request for something still local comes back fast.
The same kind of request for something that's already moved away comes back dramatically slower, even though nothing about asking for it changed at all.
There's a second subtlety worth separating out cleanly.
One setting controls how long a segment's local copy sticks around on disk.
A completely different setting controls how long that data exists anywhere at all, and shrinking the first one no longer shrinks the second.
Here's the limit this whole mechanism runs into, and the reason behind it.
Once a segment is moved away, the system treats its bytes as fixed forever.
A log that keeps rewriting its own segments in place breaks that assumption outright, which is exactly why the two features can't be turned on together.
Every number in this reel so far came from one real run of this topic's own toy tiered-storage model, happening just now.
Which segments ended up where, the fast read against the slow one, side by side.
And the rejection itself, confirmed directly rather than just asserted.
So: a closed segment moves itself the instant it closes, on its own clock, not when disk space gets tight.
Keeping it around locally and keeping it around at all are two separate settings now, not one.
Reads stay exactly as simple as before — they just aren't all equally fast anymore.
